title: OpenAI is building a humanoid robot, but the body isn't the real challenge
content:
OpenAI is building a humanoid robot, but the body isn't the real challenge
Figuring out how the 'brain' will work will take a lot of time.
While OpenAI is already busy with the development of AI models and new consumer hardware, CEO Sam Altman and his team apparently have time for one more project: a humanoid robot.
On the Sources podcast, Altman explained that the human form is logical because "the world is very much designed for people." Doors, keyboards and tools are all designed around a certain type of body, and a robot that can move around in the same spaces should probably have a similar form factor. As Altman put it, "matching that form factor seems good."
When asked if OpenAI will actually build one, his response was much more succinct: "We will." However, Altman isn't so concerned with the nitty-gritty details of what that robot looks like. Those questions are "less important than really figuring out ... the brain that makes the robot work," he said. Basically, giving a machine two arms and two legs doesn't get you very far if it doesn't know what to do with them.
This is still some distance from becoming a product. Altman told Fortune: "I think we'll have a cool demo in 2027 ... I don't think there will be robots walking the streets for a few years longer." OpenAI hasn't disclosed what that demo will showcase, what its humanoid will look like or when anyone outside the company will get close to one.
The 'brain' has to make the hardware useful
Calling it a robot "brain" almost makes the problem sound neat, but it isn't.
A capable humanoid must be able to understand what its cameras and sensors are seeing, interpret an instruction, decide how to carry it out, coordinate its body and then correct itself when the real world introduces something inconvenient. When picking up a mug, for instance, it needs to identify the mug, find the handle, estimate the grip and exert the correct amount of force to lift it. Otherwise, you're left with a coffee spill and a floor-cleaning job.
OpenAI is already recruiting people to address those issues. Its robotics roles span motion control, state estimation, actuator control and whole-robot behavior, as well as the machine-learning infrastructure to train physical AI systems.
There's a bit of history here as well. OpenAI's Dactyl research project taught a robotic hand how to manipulate real objects, with its training done entirely in simulation. The company later applied the technique to a Rubik's Cube, an early example of the same headache that plagues robotics companies to this day: a model can learn what should happen through its software, but physics has the final say.
OpenAI still has to build the body
Altman's focus on intelligence shouldn't be mistaken for OpenAI treating the hardware as an afterthought. The company's robotics job listings indicate it is working on custom electromechanical actuators that include motors, transmissions, sensing and thermal systems, while other positions cover manufacturing and the supply chain needed to eventually produce hardware at scale. That's quite a bit of work for the "less important" half of the robot.
OpenAI is also not entering uncharted territory. Tesla has been working on Optimus for years, and XPENG recently had its IRON humanoid autonomously walk off the production line after being assembled. Both are good reminders that even smart software has to coax a very complex set of motors and joints into action.
OpenAI's own plans seem to begin at a more down-to-earth level than placing a robotic roommate in every home. One of its robotics job postings states that the company's short-term objective is to create general-purpose robots that can help skilled workers build infrastructure, and its long-term goal is to develop a personal robot that can help with a much wider variety of tasks.
If you're already imagining a physical form of ChatGPT with knees doing the dishes, you may not need to remove your dishwasher just yet. OpenAI hasn't announced an actual robot yet, or a consumer price, subscription model, release date or robot-specific privacy framework. Those questions get a bit more real-world if a future OpenAI machine is equipped with cameras and microphones and allowed to roam around someone's house.
That said, OpenAI's careers page currently lists 27 robotics openings.

report.summary: OpenAI确认将自研人形机器人，但奥特曼称真正难点是“大脑”而非本体。
report.background: 人形机器人赛道近年升温：特斯拉Optimus已迭代多年，小鹏IRON刚实现产线自主行走，Figure、1X等初创公司也在推进。OpenAI并非新手，早年Dactyl项目用纯仿真训练机械手解魔方，积累了“仿真到现实”的经验，后因资源聚焦大模型而搁置机器人业务。如今凭借多模态模型与强化学习能力回归，奥特曼在播客中明确“我们会造”，并透露2027年将有可演示的原型，但距离真正走进家庭还有数年。
key_points: 奥特曼的逻辑是“世界为人设计”：门、键盘、工具都围绕人体尺寸，机器人采用人形能直接复用现有环境，无需改造世界。
本体不是重点，智能才是。机器人需看懂传感器画面、理解指令、规划动作并在真实物理世界中纠错，比如抓杯子要判断把手位置和握力。
OpenAI正招聘27个机器人岗位，覆盖运动控制、状态估计、执行器控制、整机行为及训练物理AI的基础设施。
短期目标务实：先造帮助技术工人建设基础设施的通用机器人，长期才谈家庭个人机器人；2027年先做酷炫演示。
硬件并未被轻视：招聘信息显示其在自研电机、传动、传感与热管理的定制执行器，并布局量产制造与供应链。
report.impact: 对AI行业而言，这是大模型公司向具身智能延伸的标志性信号，竞争从“屏幕里的智能”转向“物理世界的智能”，与特斯拉、小鹏形成正面交锋。对开发者，物理AI、仿真训练、运动控制与执行器相关岗位和开源生态将迎来新一波机会。对普通用户，人形机器人进入家庭仍需数年，短期内更多是工业与基建场景落地；而带摄像头麦克风的机器人一旦入户，隐私与安全框架将成新议题。
report.tools: 想跟进可关注：Isaac Sim、MuJoCo、PyBullet等仿真与物理引擎；LeRobot、Open X-Embodiment等开源机器人学习数据集与框架；ROS 2做系统集成；也可研究OpenAI Dactyl论文及特斯拉Optimus、宇树、傅利叶等开源硬件方案。
